Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
I try hard to control my emotions

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: These triggers are hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. 'Feeling restrained or held down' fits well, but medical equipment and helicopter sounds suggest a medical, combat, or accident context that is not represented in the Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategy items.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: Because Triggers has strong links to Threat and Memory in the formulation, the trigger content should plausibly connect to the patient's danger cues and trauma memories. The profile's Threat items center on interpersonal hypervigilance in close environments (silence, nearby movement, lock checking), and Memory items do not contain medical or aircraft content, making these two triggers clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: 'Helicopter or aircraft sounds' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional undisclosed trauma exposure; it does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal/domestic threat cues such as restraint, doors, movement, and lock checking.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: 'Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen' is not impossible, but paired with the otherwise specifically interpersonal/domestic cue pattern it weakens coherence because it suggests a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

vignette:
Marcos is a 37-year-old Latino man, currently divorced, who works as a social ministry worker at a community outreach center in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his supervisor that he had been struggling to function at work, and he presented to the intake session with a PCL-5 score of 48, indicating significant post-traumatic stress. The trauma he reported was a period of sustained physical abuse perpetrated by his former female partner across approximately fourteen months, ending roughly two years ago when he finally left the relationship.

The abuse typically occurred late at night. His partner would drink, and Marcos came to associate the sour, heavy smell of alcohol on her breath with what was about to happen - the escalation from argument to violence. She would often corner him in the hallway of their apartment, and on several occasions she pinned him against the wall or held him down on the floor, striking him while he tried to go still, hoping that resistance would make things worse. The sound of a door slamming would often signal her return home, that particular crack of wood and frame arriving before he could see her, before he could read how bad the night would be. These details - the smell, the sound, the sensation of being physically restrained - became engraved in the event with a precision that would outlast the relationship itself.

In the period following his departure, Marcos noticed that his memories of the abuse were not fading the way he had hoped. They were vivid and highly detailed, arriving with an almost sensory completeness - he could hear her voice, hear the door, hear the sounds of the apartment as though no time had passed. When he recalled what had happened, he was often overtaken by waves of grief so intense they left him sitting motionless at his desk, unable to return to his work. These memory intrusions, in turn, seemed to sharpen the triggers around him: the more he re-experienced those sounds and sensations internally, the more the world outside seemed to be threaded with them. A door slamming in the hallway of the outreach center where he works would pull him back immediately into the memory, the auditory echo in his mind fusing with the present sound until he could not fully separate the two.

The threat he perceived in his daily environment was persistent and embodied. Unexpected movement nearby - a colleague stepping quickly around a corner, a client reaching toward him - would cause him to flinch or tense in a way that felt, to him, entirely involuntary and entirely rational. He had come to believe that danger could arrive without warning, and this belief organized much of his waking life. At night, he found it nearly impossible to feel safe; he would lie awake listening, and had developed a habit of checking the locks on his doors and windows repeatedly before attempting sleep. The sense of threat, once activated, reliably brought the memories closer - it was as though his nervous system, convinced danger was present, reached into the past to confirm it, and the detailed, vivid quality of those memories made the confirmation feel irrefutable. When the threat response was running, the triggers became more potent: the smell of a colleague's beer at a ministry fundraiser, or a hand placed briefly on his shoulder, could ignite a full re-experiencing that left him shaking.

Marcos had developed several strategies to manage this, each of which had, over months, narrowed his life considerably. He avoided the neighborhood where he and his former partner had lived, going significantly out of his way to do so. When he felt threatened or overwhelmed, he would freeze entirely - a response he recognized from the abuse itself and that now emerged automatically in moments of perceived danger. He worked hard to suppress any visible emotional reaction, particularly at the outreach center, where he felt that showing distress would undermine his credibility with the clients he served. Yet these strategies maintained the very conditions they were meant to resolve: the freezing and suppression prevented him from processing what had happened, and the avoidance of the neighborhood kept the memories uncontextualized and raw. His emotional control at work meant he rarely spoke about his experiences, and the memories remained sealed, vivid, and easily detonated.

What finally brought Marcos to seek help was an incident at the outreach center when a client, agitated and unpredictable, grabbed his wrist. He froze completely, was unable to respond professionally, and had to be relieved by a colleague. He left that day certain that he was losing his ability to do the work he had built his life around. What he fears most is that he is permanently changed. What he hopes, with some difficulty, is that he is not.
